title: [OPINION] How did the Philippine government perform at COP31?
summary: Any COP pavilion is worth it if it translates pledges into grants, investments, and other finance that does not burden Filipinos

blocks.text: Any COP pavilion is worth it if it translates pledges into grants, investments, and other finance that does not burden Filipinos

Unknown to millions of Filipinos preoccupied with the ASEAN Summit and the latest controversies hitting the Marcos Jr. administration, the future of the country was being shaped at a more important conference thousands of kilometers away.

At the recent 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, the Philippine government launched a set of new plans and frameworks that would redefine the direction of national climate action for at least the next decade.
At the Philippine Hub (the country’s pavilion at COP31), the government presented to the global community the following major plans:

items: The 2026 Nationally Determined Contribution, which states that the country will avoid and reduce its emissions by 75% within the next decade;
The Just Transition Framework, which charts the nation’s pathway of low-emissions, climate-resilient development where no one is left behind;
The Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework, which aims to accelerate climate change mitigation through market-based mechanisms that attract more investments; and
The Philippine Climate Finance Strategy, which outlines how the nation will secure finance from public and private sectors, here and abroad.

blocks.text: This is not to mention findings from notable studies on health, inequality, energy, climate budget, and other issues from both government and nongovernmental groups.

These are plans and frameworks many sectors — civil society, private sector, development partners, and even other government agencies — have helped shape to varying extents and have been waiting to be finalized for years.

These launches were done at the Philippine Hub to directly inform COP31 — which has at least 92,000 participants, the most in history — that the country has never been more ready to accelerate its climate solutions.

With global warming set to exceed the long-term goal of 1.5 degrees Celsius under the Paris Agreement in the near future, it is critical for the Philippines to not only show institutional readiness to implement its own solutions but also scale up its responses to protect its vulnerable communities and ecosystems.
To give credit where it’s due, compared to a few years ago, the conduct of the Philippine Hub was relatively more inclusive. There is room for improvement, but that is worth recognizing.

Nevertheless, it is also necessary to examine whether all of these new plans and frameworks are sufficient to align the Philippines with the 1.5°C goal. It is part of the nation’s equitable responsibility as part of the ruling under the International Court of Justice Advisory Opinion on climate change released in 2025. But another question is worth reflecting on.

At COP30 in Brazil in 2025, the Philippines was criticized by many, including civil society groups, for not having its own pavilion compared to its ASEAN neighbors. This year, around P23 million was set under the 2026 General Appropriations Act to ensure the country would have its own space to conduct side events, meetings, and the launching of plans and frameworks.

It is understandable to be skeptical about such expenditures, especially given the nation’s economic state, the lingering aftermath of the flood control corruption scandal, and the numerous crises it faces, including the climate one. This is also considering that COP31 failed to even produce a major agreement — the first time since 2009, coincidentally when the Philippines enacted the Climate Change Act.
Unfortunately, COP pavilions have become notoriously expensive over the years, with larger country pavilions costing about twice as much.

Yet it did not stop other vulnerable countries, especially small Pacific island nations, from securing their own pavilions. They understand the need to send powerful messages of hope and progress through their spaces and to keep the pressure on developed countries and polluters to pay up, in one way or another.
This is why context matters; on that note, it is necessary for the Philippines to have a COP pavilion. The question of whether it was worth the cost is an entirely different discussion.

Any COP pavilion is worth it if it translates pledges into grants, investments, and other finance that does not burden Filipinos. It is worth it if all the launched plans and reports in those two weeks lead to reduced emissions, vulnerabilities, and losses and damages, enhanced climate resilience, and other benefits felt on the ground.

These messages were also mentioned by three of the country’s lead negotiators: Robert Borje (co-head of delegation and overall co-facilitator on finance), Yolando Velasco (on finance), and Noralene Uy (on adaptation) during side events at the Philippine Hub.

Borje also highlighted during the closing plenary the necessity of finance in enabling implementation of solutions that developing countries like the Philippines need, although there is uncertainty as to whether the country was favoring or rejecting the adoption of the proposed cover decision text.

Every word said in side events, every named partner plastered on its walls, every commitment to be made — everything about what the Philippine government does at climate COPs must be grounded in the pursuit of climate justice for the most vulnerable.
As challenging as engaging in climate COPs is, a significant issue remains: there is some misalignment between what the government pushes for in the negotiations and what is happening back home.

This must be addressed if we don’t want another failure like the flood control corruption scandal to happen again. Polluters must pay, including those who hinder renewable energy development because they don’t think it’s profitable. Communities must be supported to claim their space in decision-making spaces and demand finance and other means of implementation to address climate impacts.

The work at COP31 is over. The Philippines has shown its cards at the world’s biggest stage. Now the next year of climate action begins. We’ll see whether words will be turned into action. – Rappler.com
